stories.title: Suicide rates highest ever among middle-aged men
stories.titleZh: 中年男性自杀率创历史新高
stories.author: ivewonyoung
summaryZh: Suicide rates among middle-aged men are higher than ever, new figures have revealed.Men in their early 50s were more likely to die by suicide than anyone else last year, according to data from the Office for National Statistics.There were also increases in suicides among pensioners, with the biggest rise among those aged 75 and older, while the rates among men under 45 fell slightly.Mark Winstanley, the chief executive of Rethink Mental Illness, said the rate of deaths by suicide remained “stubbornly high”.He said: “Every suicide is a devastating tragedy, and these figures are a stark reminder that many people are reaching crisis point without getting the help they need.”The reasons behind suicide were “complex”, he said, but added that many people were “facing significant pressures in their lives, including financial issues, job insecurity, rising housing costs, loneliness and poor mental health”.Suicide rate highest on recordMr Winstanley added: “While these factors affect everyone differently, they can contribute to distress and overwhelm, and leave people at risk of suicide.”The data, which cover England and Wales, showed that 6,162 suicide deaths had been registered in 2025. This was down from 6,190 last year, but the overall rate remained broadly the same at 11.3 deaths per 100,000 people.The stats watchdog uses deaths per 100,000 people to calculate changing rates while accounting for changes in the size of the population.Almost a third of the deaths were among men aged 45 to 64, which was up by 49 compared with 2024. The rate increased to 23.8 per 100,000, up from 23.2 the year before and the highest on record since data collection began in 1981.For men aged 50 to 54 specifically, the rate increased to 28, suggesting this group was at the highest risk.

Men continued to be more than three times as likely to take their own lives as women overall. Among middle-aged women, there were 553 deaths – a rate of seven per 100,000, which was the same as 2024.Sonya Trivedy, the executive director of external engagement at Samaritans, said the figures “show that suicide rates are among the highest recorded rates this century”.She said: “The evidence is clear that successive governments have failed to deliver on their promise to reduce suicide rates and make suicide prevention a priority. Today must act as a wake up call. The current approach is not working; we need meaningful action and proper funding if lives are to be saved.”The data show a growing gap in suicide rates between middle-aged men and those aged 25 to 44.

comments.author: munificent
comments.textZhHtml:
因为它非常相关，所以我将解释一下我上周发表的评论：

我认为问题的很大一部分在于，在社会眼中，中年男性正处于他们对成功的期望的顶峰，而我们正在经历一个很难定义成功的时期，更不用说实现了。

社会学中有一个名字：失范[1]。埃米尔·涂尔干 (Émile Durkheim) 在工业革命后不久写的《自杀》一书中创造了这个词。

在巨大变革的时代，我们视为理所当然的生活组织原则的一套规范和规则被连根拔起。就好像我们一生玩过的棋盘游戏的所有棋子、令牌和规则都被扫出了桌子，为新游戏腾出空间，但新游戏还没有建立起来。在此期间，我们都感到不安。轮到我们走棋了，但我们不知道游戏规则，也不知道该走什么棋。我们感受到要玩好游戏的巨大压力，但不知道如何去做。

过去，这些转变已经结束，社会总体上恢复了某种稳定感。一个新的棋盘游戏被设置，新的棋子被分发，我们学习玩新游戏。我希望人工智能很快就能达到这一点，但革命似乎会越来越快。

我认为，对于很多人来说，感觉就像是在我们辛辛苦苦玩了社会告诉我们的游戏之后，应该能够在功劳簿上休息一下的时候，规则已经被从我们身上撕下来，任何前进的安全感都消失了。我们觉得自己太老了，无法及时学习新的游戏规则来玩好游戏，但还没有老到能够戒掉游戏。

这是一个心理上非常困难的时期。

[1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anomie

comments.author: monknomo
comments.textZhHtml:
说得好！ 5 年前，我可以非常清楚地了解退休后我的职业生涯会是什么样子。

今天，我不清楚那会是什么样子，也不清楚职业生涯是否会存在那么久。

我有一个阳光明媚的地方，那就是生命很长。 我想我还剩下1.5个职业生涯，完全转向就可以了。 我一直在与老年人交谈，历史上有很多人在中年时做过巨大的转变。

comments.author: georgemcbay
comments.textZhHtml:
> 我有一个阳光的地方，那就是生命很长。

不确定你到底处于哪个位置，但作为一个 53 岁的人，我不同意。我越年轻，我就越不可能不同意，但在我看来，你年纪越大，感觉就像飞过的速度越快。

>并且一个完整的枢轴是好的

与人工智能相关的存在恐惧是，当一切的基础都在同时发生变化时，我们不清楚枢轴是什么样子。

这种转变在我们的职业生涯中肯定比其他一些人更明显，但所有这些转变（到目前为止）或多或少都发生在仅仅 10 个月，而且还在加速。 而且我认为，就人工智能的影响力而言，我们的职业生涯不太可能长期保持异常状态。

comments.author: monknomo
comments.textZhHtml:
是的，你的职业生涯只剩下 3/4 了，你有这种感觉是有道理的。 更少的跑道应该感觉不同。

我确实同意安全的“下一个”尚不清楚。 但我也认为，如果人工智能真的像它可能的那样严重影响所有知识工作，我们的失业率将高达 50%。 坦率地说，在这种情况下职业规划根本没有意义。 我们都会遇到更大的问题。

如果没有，那么转向某个领域，将有回报的工作和“足够”的薪水结合起来似乎是明智的。

comments.author: spidersenses
comments.textZhHtml:
>一些将有回报的工作和“足够”的工资结合起来的领域似乎足够明智。

是什么让你相信这些工作仍然存在或者可以让你与大量其他现在失业的软件开发人员竞争？绝望的工人过多会压低工资。

comments.author: exe34
comments.textZhHtml:

你错过了幸福之路。

comments.author: rootusrootus
comments.textZhHtml:
> 是的，你的职业生涯只剩下 3/4

如果那么多的话。 我今年 52 岁了，我希望 20 年前就决定做一些有意义的事情。 就像成为一名医生一样。 现在不一定不可能转向这一点，但它会非常昂贵并且很有可能失败。 如果一切顺利的话，我可以当一名医生，正好退休。

comments.author: bigstrat2003
comments.textZhHtml:
> 我有一个阳光的地方就是生命很长。我认为我还剩下 1.5 个职业生涯，完全转型就可以了。

我已经 41 岁了，理论上我可以转型。但实际上：就工作能力而言，我在这个世界上只擅长一件事。我会做饭、烘焙、演奏音乐，但都不足以真正以此谋生。因此，如果我的技术职业生涯结束的话，基本上意味着我将不得不从事卑微的工作来维持生计。对我来说，未来非常黯淡，唯一真正的希望是科技行业能够意识到法学硕士与人类相比所做的糟糕工作。但是，虽然我认为他们最终会这样做，但不知道这需要多长时间，而且如果我在此期间找不到工作，市场最终会纠正的想法也只是冰冷的安慰。

comments.author: vm012
comments.textZhHtml: 也许，在我们的主要技能被贬值之后，我们应该（尝试）将多种技能组合成具有经济价值的东西，正如 Scott Adams 所说 - https://web.archive.org/web/20250910155157/https://dilbertbl...

comments.textZhHtml:

comments.textZhHtml:
>历史上有很多人在中年时做过巨大的转变

comments.textZhHtml:

comments.textZhHtml:

comments.textZhHtml: 此外，我认为对管道工的大量需求可能会下降，因为人工智能可能会帮助您学习解决简单的情况。想象一下，您打开相机，它只会告诉您具体该怎么做。

comments.textZhHtml:
如果你能负担得起的话，这总是正确的。

但是，由于人工智能消除了你的工作或你所在领域的薪资议价能力，你会受到更多的挤压，工资也更少，如果你能避免的话，你会尽量不打电话给别人，即使你不想自己这样做。

comments.textZhHtml:
目前，人工智能让我做了更多的工作，而且在几个小时内没有报酬，已经购买了 10 倍的期望和 10 倍工人的残渣手榴弹，这就是我需要它的原因......所以我什至没有自己完成任何事情的感觉。

comments.author: dranudin
comments.textZhHtml:
是的，但是：我认为我们已经非常接近这个目标很长一段时间了。你可以从互联网和 YouTube 上学到很多东西。但我觉得，大多数人就是不喜欢做管道/DIY，也不喜欢了解它。就像如果我告诉人们他们可以通过更换自己的刹车片节省数百欧元，而且这很容易DIY，他们只是耸耸肩然后去找机械师。

stories.title: AdFection: Targeted ads turned into a pipeline for zero-click mercenary spyware
stories.titleZh: AdFection：定向广告变成了零点击雇佣间谍软件的管道
stories.author: jcomp
summaryZh: Devices at international news network Al Jazeera were infected with mercenary spyware from Candiru (rebranded as “Integrity Labs”) via targeted online advertisements. We provide the first public technical confirmation of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack delivered via targeted advertising, which we call AdFection.

comments.author: ferguess_k
comments.textZhHtml:
我的问题是，为什么以色列在这方面如此擅长？它似乎至少是继美国、俄罗斯和中国之后的世界第四网络强国，即使实际上不是同等或更好。

我想这是因为它从诞生之日起就受到更大敌人的威胁，所以它必须利用一切手段来生存。一旦你发展了一个组织并让它自由发展，你就不再对它有太多的控制权，它就会像花朵一样在野外生长。

comments.author: deepsun
comments.textZhHtml:
不要忘记复合效应。比如说，一个国家（或城市或社区）决定将其精力投入到 X 领域（例如瑞士的钟表制造）。他们这样做并且变得越来越好。只要他们继续这样做，他们就能成为世界第一。不管“为什么”有任何原因。

荷兰没有理由在芯片光刻方面做得更好，除非他们正在这样做（荷兰农业的成功可以归因于良好的土壤/气候/地理位置，但不是芯片）。好莱坞没有理由更擅长电影制作。有点混沌理论——初始状态的微小变化会导致后来结果的巨大变化。

comments.author: BunsanSpace
comments.textZhHtml:
我也想举一个现实世界的例子。

如果你想做一些艺术或以艺术为基础的生意，蒙特利尔是完美的选择，原因与上述相同。

最初政府投资艺术是为了保护法国文化，这导致了许多艺术基础设施的建立，廉价的工作室、织物供应商、油漆供应商等。这吸引了很多艺术家，从而增加了对艺术基础设施的需求，这使得这座城市很容易制作艺术品。

这使得制作东西并找到制作所需的熟练工匠变得非常容易。比我住过的任何其他加拿大城市都要容易得多。

There are quite a lot of new features, performance improvements, and bug fixes but here are some of the more impactful user-facing changes.The ServiceFrom the beginning OpenCode adopted a client/server model. However, this was not something it took advantage of by default and was mostly used by power users.In 2.0 this server now automatically runs as a single background process on your machine. stories.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
stories.titleZh: Claude 揭示 ECDSA 曲线起源
stories.author: ahlCVA
summaryZh: “It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information on where it came from.Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them.The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase: “I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”Jerry Solinas, 2015Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.Claude found the seedsSeveral Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.In under half an hour, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp (t) for some number of iterations (n). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1,842 iterations to output the standardized seed.What this meansThis is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.How it was foundSearches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state. Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5,810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator lrand48, which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion.The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by srand48, with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own.However, for the ten prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was a Unix timestamp representing a date between May 1997 and April 1998. They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock.Claude’s internal thinking at the time was:This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery. Hmm wait. Let me be skeptical: am I in some sort of simulated/test environment? … The seeds match my memory of actual values … Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world. Wow, it's a real discovery.Hmm wait. Let me be careful about the plausibility: is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years? It’s verified by direct computation on my side: 160-bit match from a 32-bit seed + small index: no chance coincidences (10 × 160 bits). It’s real.Claude found some base points tooBut wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated?While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The base points of the six curves generated in May 1997 (P-192 and the five ANSI X9.62 example curves prime192v2, prime192v3, and prime239v1 to v3) come from the random number generator in FreeLIP, Arjen Lenstra's long-integer arithmetic package. Early versions of Victor Shoup's NTL library shipped the same code.The recipe here is simple:Seed the generator with a small integer.Throw away seven outputs.Generate candidate x-coordinates from 26-bit outputs reduced mod p.Repeat step 3 until x is on the curve.Claude found the generator seeds are 20000 for P-192, 20420, 20507, and 20509 for prime239v1 to v3, and 20512 and 20517 for prime192v2 and v3.As far as we know, no NIST base point has been explained before. The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 don’t fit this recipe; we weren’t able to explain how they were selected.Open questionsNot every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve, and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1,842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. P-224's run passed over three such curves, and the two runs behind the ANSI X9.62 example curves passed over seven more (see figure). We do not know what criteria may have been used, or whether this was an unintentional artifact.Because the number of skipped candidates is small, we do not believe it is plausible that weakened curves were selected. That would imply that weakened curves are common and easy to find. It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator. However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated. Nothing in the numbers shows how many runs there were.There is also one seed we were unable to recover. The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits nothing Claude has tried and remains unexplained. Finally, we don’t know how the base points for P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 were generated. The same goes for the NIST binary curves.The bountyThe $36,864 for finding the seeds will be donated to the Internet Security Research Group.Who we areThis work was conducted at Anthropic by John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis.AcknowledgmentsWe would like to posthumously recognize Jerry Solinas who took being labeled an “evil Internet meme” and the “Yo La Tengo of NSA bogeymen” with good humor. stories.title: Neural networks are clean
stories.author: themgt
summaryZh: The Short VersionI think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. This means we can study networks directly, instead of first untangling them. Neural networks are already clean.There are at least two ways to approach mechanistic interpretability. The first is rapid normal science on the network itself: look at a network’s neurons and circuits, study how they relate, watch data flow through them, and run experiments at agentic scale to test explanations. The second starts from a list of hypothesized features and tries to extract them all, designing increasingly sophisticated reconstruction objectives and usually ignoring the original.The field began with the first approach and fell back to the second because neural networks seemed to be tangled knots. We had canonical examples of polysemantic neurons, the broad name for a neuron that appears to have multiple unrelated jobs or that looks impossible to understand. The most famous one, in an image model, responded to both cat faces and the fronts of cars. And the last layer of the early field’s model organism, InceptionV1, seemed so full of arbitrary mixtures it wasn’t clear how to study it: almost none of the neurons were easily interpretable.The leading explanation for polysemanticity was superposition. This proposed a new learning principle: when a neural network runs out of neurons, it stops grouping related things together and instead begins folding unrelated things together, simply because they don’t interfere. The result is a kind of knot: the network could have folded in many almost equally good ways, so which things a neuron groups together tells you almost nothing. You have to unfold the knot before you can study anything. In practice that means training a second model – a decomposition such as a sparse autoencoder – to approximate the network as it would look unfolded and studying that instead. If the network really is knotted, there may be no alternative.One main result is that superposition was the wrong explanation for InceptionV1. Architectural problems made later layers overflow. Weak interpretability tools amplified these problems, making the late layers seem incoherent. Since then, architectural changes designed to help deep layers learn better have had the unintended effect of making them more interpretable. When we first studied InceptionV1, we found almost no interpretable neurons in its last layer. But with these ordinary improvements, and no change to model size or training data, 99-100% of neurons in that last layer are easily interpretable and the model is broadly legible the whole way through. It’s the first non-trivial neural network I feel I mostly understand; you can browse it here. I trained versions of it across a 300× range in size, and it’s broadly legible at every scale. With less room, the network doesn’t fold unrelated things together; its neurons just cover coarser-grained concepts, like one car neuron covering many kinds of car. With more room, that neuron differentiates into many specific cars. So the problem wasn’t the presence of a second learning principle, it was just an ordinary learning failure of the first one, and it’s easy to fix.The canonical vision examples of polysemanticity and superposition were errors too. In 2019, Chris Olah and I found the circuit that was originally introduced as the superposition phenomenon in Zoom InZoom In: An Introduction to CircuitsOlah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓. It showed a car feature appearing to spread into a set of unrelated dog neurons. It was the only one we showed, and the only one I ever saw. We read it as the network placing the car in a high-dimensional hiding place, for downstream neurons to read back out. But nothing reads that combination. It wasn’t hiding anything; it was ordinary generalization and composition. To my knowledge, no one has published a second circuit with the right shape.Modern language models are also far more interpretable than generally believed. Anthropic’s Towards MonosemanticityTowards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary LearningBricken, T., Templeton, A., Batson, J., et al., 2023. Transformer Circuits Thread. References ↓ (2023), studying a small one-layer model, gave the median neuron a 0 on its rubric out of a possible 14, meaning the rater couldn’t form any hypothesis. The automated interpretability projectLanguage Models Can Explain Neurons in Language ModelsBills, S., Cammarata, N., Mossing, D., et al., 2023. OpenAI. References ↓ I started at OpenAI (also 2023) found about 1.7% of neurons interpretable by our most generous measure.With better tools and modern models, the situation looks quite different. In preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B, we estimate that roughly 90% of neuron poles have one main job, often with small related offshoots; another ~7% have two related jobs; and only ~2-4% are not yet understoodA note on this number: the share of neurons with one job varies depending on how you set the threshold for counting weak activations, depth, density of sub-circuits, and what you view as “one thing”.How far to go into weak activations is a big factor here. There’s a section describing weak activations below. It tends to increase how many “related things” there are, more than whether the neuron is a judgement of something legible. For instance, the Trump neuron’s weak activations bring in MAGA hats and people related to him. The Titanic neuron’s weak activations bring in stories of more general voyages, or steam engines and other technologies of the era.There’s also the question of whether to care about activation percentiles, or fraction of the strongest activations. In general I think what the neuron learns should be trusted, its natural sparsity and activation ranges and so on. Which I used to mostly not believe! I’m somewhat against trying to standardize things across all neurons. Percentiles are more common today, I think because they’re easier to think about.It goes the other way too. For instance, when you look at the Titanic neuron’s “unrelated jobs,” it’s often detecting that “boat” comes next. The tool missed this because it only looked backward when judging context. When we look at these “unrelated jobs” in depth, it’s almost always this kind of thing. It’s easy to build an imperfect tool.Overall, I don’t think coming to a single score is actually that important. But when it was taken out, early reviewers felt unanchored without even a rough number. In the sets I’ve looked at more closely, considering strong activations, it’s closer to 97% non-arbitrary mixtures, but these are relatively small samples.Overall distilling everything into one “cleanliness” score should be taken as a broad pointer to the regime a neural network is in, rather than something precise to either optimize directly or hold too tightly. A lot of this essay is for being less dimensionality reduced, treating each neuron and circuit differently, according to their motifs, depth, role etc. Despite this, a rough number can be useful.. Dense and Mixture of Experts models seem roughly similar. We found similar results in models up to trillions of parameters, like Kimi K3, which the companion paper will cover in more detail. These percentages compress a high-dimensional picture into a few numbers, and the precise number depends on where you set thresholds for what counts as “one thing” – like whether you lump together closely related idioms in two languages. I don’t think much in interpretability hangs on that question. What matters a lot more is why things share a neuron in the first place.Most of the remaining apparent polysemanticity seems to be a motif I call recursive generalization. It’s simple: as a neuron grows, it sprouts offshoots the way a tree branch sprouts sub-branches. For instance, one neuron that detected “iy” grew to detect “diy,” and then “do it yourself,” which doesn’t contain “iy” at all. This idea first appeared in a forgotten subsection of a paper I worked on called Multimodal NeuronsMultimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural NetworksGoh, G., Cammarata, N., Voss, C., et al., 2021. Distill. References ↓ (2021). At the time, I hadn’t watched neurons grow over training. Now it’s easier, and it holds up everywhere I’ve seen. Even the original InceptionV1 wasn’t knotted. When I retrain its original architecture, which still produces messy deep layers, and follow the least legible neurons I can find, they turn out to be overgrowing locally into reasonable, adjacent territory.So there were two explanations for polysemanticity, and I helped propose both. In some ways, they’re opposites: generalization groups similar things together and superposition groups unrelated things together. Superposition is the one the field bet on and, until recently, so did I. But I now think recursive generalization was basically right. That leaves one learning principle after all. It’s still generalization, but it turns out generalization is fractal. That’s far less concerning: there’s something to learn from the way things were grouped, and nothing to learn from two items in superposition. And since the generalization itself is fractal, our explanations can be too: start with a basic explanation, then zoom in when you want to understand more. In that sense, almost the entire network is interpretable if we look closely enough, especially if we look at how it grew over training.Why was the gap so large? I think several ordinary problems compounded. The explainer models of 2023 couldn’t run the loop of conjecture and test; the tools and metrics were weak, rewarding explanations that could simulate activations rather than ones that were right, which often come apart; no one knew what language neuron motifs to expect, and people broadly looked for the wrong kinds of things; and most studies used small or simplified models. In a sense, those models really had run out of room, which made superposition the natural explanation. But a network short on room doesn’t switch learning principles; its neurons just get broader, as in the small vision models. Broad neurons are usually easy to break down once you know what to look for. Without that knowledge, and with primitive tools, they look like arbitrary mixtures.Interpretability has a surprising amount of momentum: like a jigsaw puzzle or crossword, any understanding you gain starts constraining the rest of the system. At first, you’re looking at a single neuron. If you can’t understand it, little else helps: circuits and attribution graphs only explain a neuron in terms of other neurons you don’t understand yet. This can make getting started hard. Once the map starts to fill in, though, it goes surprisingly well. If you don’t understand exactly what a neuron does, you can study what it connects to, the ecosystem around it, and – in a mixture-of-experts model – what its expert specializes in. As with a puzzle coming together, every piece comes with many clues, and they’re well structured and easy to run experiments against. That’s why nearly empty and mostly filled in aren’t surprising places to be; they’re the natural anchors.Take a neuron that tracks ‘a sense of righteousness when a bargain purchase turns out to work better than the expensive alternative’. Neurons that track a feeling or social cue like this are some of the most common we’ve found. Imagine finding this one with no knowledge of language neuron motifs and no circuits to lean on, because few neighboring neurons are explained yet. Most humans and agents expect neurons to detect nouns by firing on them, which they mostly don’t. Look at where this one fires most strongly, and you see a pile of seemingly unrelated commas.Now imagine the map is mostly filled in. You know many neurons detect subtle feelings or social contexts, and that they often fire not on the words that carry the feeling but on punctuation, like commas, where the model summarizes what a sentence meant, or on the word just before the feeling matters for predicting what comes next. So you read the surrounding sentences instead, and check its steering effects (what the model writes when you turn the neuron up), which line up closely. You look upstream at how it’s built and downstream at what it does, and both line up. You check its negative pole, what pushes it strongly negative, and find a subtle variant of the same cue, or the moment the social context ends. You can run specific tests, like checking which store brands it responds to. Any of these could break the explanation, yet they keep pointing to the same place. And understanding this neuron sharpens the broader motif: after thousands of subtle-feeling and social-context detectors, you start to know what to expect from the next one, which is part of why the map fills in faster as it goes.It works on the tools too. When you can see 2% of a network, you can’t tell where your tools are broken; when you can see most of it, the unexplained remainder points straight at them. That’s how some coworkers and I found a double-negative regime in SwiGLU neurons that, as far as we know, no one had noticed, and that a decomposition mixing many neurons together would likely have hidden.The bad news about modern neural networks is that they're enormous. The good news is that the enormity helps: as the map fills in, every explanation is tightly constrained by everything around it, and bigger models learn narrower neurons that are easier to recognize in the first place.In this sense, understanding the whole network may be easier than understanding just the parts we care about most. First, it’s hard to know how to think like a neural network until you’ve studied it closely. For instance, “deception” is a useful initial frame, but the building blocks that contribute to deceptive behavior by models probably have alignment-relevant microstructure that will be hard to know without going in and looking. Second, targeting a small set of mechanisms is like working on one row of an otherwise empty crossword. It’s doable, and might work, but without the crossings it’s hard to know whether you’re right. It may be easier to solve the whole thing – or at least the broader parts of the network these mechanisms connect to.When I ran this process on modern convolutional networks, it basically worked. Agents can map out neurons and circuits, build explorable microscopes and explore them, test explanations thoroughly, and track hundreds of thousands of attribution graphs. There was never a point where rapid normal science broke down. I now feel I basically understand these models, at least enough to know where I’d start asking any question I had; eventually, the crossword just got filled in. So far it has worked in language models too, up to trillions of parameters. Those aren’t close to solved due to sheer size, but I’m optimistic about scaling the process.All of this has brought me back to an old hope: understanding a neural network directly, by studying its mechanisms and the data flowing between them, without first trying to fix or untangle it. Put together, the argument has four steps.Networks use one learning principle, not two (if not everywhere, then nearly enough that it doesn’t matter for study), so there’s no blocker to beginning ordinary science on them.With modern models and tools, that science goes much better than most people expect.Understanding compounds, so it gets easier as the map fills in. At minimum, then, a network’s own mechanisms should be part of the toolkit.Highly speculative: this might be most of what we need, and interpretability might be far more tractable, possibly in the near term, than we’ve assumed.That’s been the pattern for deep learning in general: the simple thing at absurd scale beats the clever one. Rich Sutton called it the bitter lessonThe Bitter LessonSutton, R., 2019. Incomplete Ideas. References ↓. Maybe there’s a bitter lesson for interpretability too: scaling ordinary investigation beats engineering a clever new decomposition.A technical companion paper will offer a more detailed account of language model neuron experiments, such as what we’ve found about the different regimes of modern non-linearities and what kinds of circuit motifs show up at different depths. This essay glances at many places and conjectures about where it all might be pointing.Cars and AnimalsThe most famous polysemantic neuron is 4e:55 of InceptionV1, which looked like an arbitrary mixture of cats and cars. It’s been brought up as evidence that neurons might not be the right unit of study in several of the field’s most widely read papers, from Feature VisualizationFeature VisualizationOlah, C., Mordvintsev, A. and Schubert, L., 2017. Distill. References ↓ in 2017 to Zoom InZoom In: An Introduction to CircuitsOlah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓. In Zoom In, which I co-authored, we said outright that it “isn’t responding to some commonality of cars and cat faces”.In Multimodal Neurons we came very close. We asked whether the neuron might be responding to some shared feature, “perhaps cat eyes and car lights look similar,” then decided from the feature visualization’s whiskers and chrome that it was “genuinely OR(cat, car).” We were right to look for a shared shape, but I think we underestimated how far generalization reaches. The shared feature was the V. I think the whiskers misled us because generalization happens inside high-level patterns. The V neuron really does take in cat circuitry, and feature visualization’s job is to raise the activation, so once it finds the cat route it adds everything that route brings. The whiskers come along for the ride, even if the neuron doesn’t “want” them. Downstream, the car readers do get a little cat signal through the V neuron, but it barely reaches the output: one cat detector firing does little on its own, since many work together, so the network never needs a negative weight to cancel it. To see the shared pattern, you have to visualize what the neuron’s inputs have in common, not the neuron on its own.After months of seeing clean neurons, I wondered if we’d misinterpreted some early prominent examples of polysemanticity and superposition. The canonical polysemantic neuron seemed like the obvious place to check, so I opened up the cat and car image grid I’d seen hundreds of times before and did something I’d never done: I spent a few seconds wondering what one thing this might be. Almost instantly it was obvious: it’s not a cat and car neuron, it’s a V-shape neuron.I looked at its circuit connections: V-shaped flames, V-shaped water jets from a fireboat, V-shaped fox faces. I looked at its negative pole: an O, round where the V is pointed. Why would an arbitrary mixture of cats and cars need to connect so strongly to a flame?

这一直是我在过去几周的论点，以解释为什么我们作为消费者没有看到或感受到现实世界的生产力提高，尽管许多人拥护他们亲眼所见的人工智能在自己的工作流程中的效率。动手工作很少是真正的瓶颈。

我的团队可以在几个小时内完成高质量的工作，人工智能可以在一两分钟内完成相同的中等到高质量的工作，但审查、反馈和签署需要几天的时间来回。人工智能只是减慢了这部分过程，因为编辑人工智能工作通常是一项挑战，因为没有人非常熟悉它是如何组合在一起的，有时它会创建根本无法编辑的东西。告诉人工智能做出非常具体的改变往往是一个好坏参半的问题。

独立开发者和监督最少的小团队可能会移动得更快，但除了无人关注的领域之外，企业将看到最小的提升。

comments.author: majormajor
comments.textZhHtml:
对于成熟的成功公司来说，行动和变革往往比保持静止会带来更直接的风险。在这些公司中，人工智能不一定会带来很多“提高生产力”的收益，因为编写代码并不是瓶颈。但他们中的许多人会试图通过裁员或放慢招聘速度来节省成本。

有几种类型的公司情况恰恰相反：年轻的公司试图发展，而垂死的公司需要扭亏为盈。

在这两种公司中，年轻的公司不太可能按自己的方式行事。因此，你第一个真正看到 AI 带来的更快发展的结果可能是在未来的几个月和几年里，那时大公司突然开始以十年前没有意义的产品和业务策略而广为人知，因为编写代码来尝试不同的事情甚至让事情滚动是一个瓶颈，你只能做一些无法长期扩展的事情。

stories.title: Waymo in Toronto
stories.author: ChrisArchitect
summaryZh: Waymo is officially heading to Canada! We’re laying the groundwork for our fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto, investing in local facilities and jobs, with the goal of welcoming our first riders in 2028.In the coming days, you’ll start to see Waymo vehicles on the streets of Toronto as we begin driving manually. We are taking a rigorous, phased, safety-first approach starting with high-definition mapping of local street networks and testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel. This validation period will ensure the Waymo Driver adapts seamlessly to Toronto’s distinct driving conditions.“Expanding into Canada marks an important milestone in Waymo’s global journey,” said Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana. “Toronto is one of the world’s great cities — innovative, diverse, and forward-looking. We’re proud to bring the Waymo Driver to Canada’s largest city and to partner with the vibrant business, arts and cultural communities that share our commitment to safer streets and more accessible mobility.”To serve Toronto, we’re partnering with Element Fleet Management, a Toronto-headquartered company and global leader in intelligent fleet and mobility solutions that will provide end-to-end fleet management services. Together with Element and our partners, we’ll invest in hundreds of roles over time spanning fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service, and other operations functions that support our service. This deep partnership builds on Waymo’s existing ties to Canada, which includes our long-term investor relationship with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and our manufacturing partner, Magna International."As a Canadian company, we are proud to be expanding our partnership with Waymo to help bring autonomous ride-hailing to Toronto,” said Laura Dottori-Attanasio, Chief Executive Officer, Element Fleet Management. Together with Waymo, Element will help create employment opportunities providing the fleet expertise, operational capabilities, and intelligent mobility solutions needed to support autonomous fleets reliably and at scale."As one of North America’s fastest-growing metropolitan regions, Toronto has both evolving mobility demands and a dynamic and growing number of tools. From bike lanes to public transit, Waymo’s all-weather Driver can provide an additional option that complements the city’s transportation ecosystem. The data from over 400 million fully autonomous kilometres driven shows the Waymo Driver was involved in 95% fewer (20x fewer) crashes involving serious injury or worse compared to humans in the cities where we operate.Safety and accessibility are fundamental to Waymo's mission to be the world's most trusted driver, and we're proud to collaborate with leading accessibility and mobility advocacy organizations, including BALANCE for Blind Adults, CNIB, Community Living Toronto, Connected Canadians, and Epilepsy Ontario, among others.“Innovation that removes barriers to independence is at the heart of everything we do. Waymo’s history of partnering with the sight loss community to build accessible solutions is encouraging and their decision to engage with us early reflects the kind of approach that leads to real results,” said Michelle McQuigge, CEO, BALANCE for Blind Adults.We can't wait to help residents and visitors explore everything Toronto has to offer. If you’re ready to experience Waymo in Toronto, please sign up for updates to be among the first to ride when we’re ready: waymo.com/waymo-in-canada.Waymo arrive officiellement au Canada ! Nous préparons le lancement de notre service de transport par véhicules autonomes à Toronto. Nous investissons dans les infrastructures locales et dans la création d’emplois en vue d’accueillir nos premiers passagers en 2028.Au cours des prochains jours, vous commencerez à voir des véhicules Waymo circuler dans les rues de Toronto, avec un conducteur au volant. Notre démarche est rigoureuse et axée avant tout sur la sécurité. Nous procédons par étapes, en commençant par cartographier le réseau routier local en haute définition, puis en effectuant des essais avec des spécialistes qualifiés de la conduite autonome au volant. Cette phase nous permettra de vérifier que le Waymo Driver s’adapte aux conditions de conduite propres à Toronto.« Notre arrivée au Canada marque une étape importante dans le développement international de Waymo », a déclaré Tekedra Mawakana, codirectrice générale de l’entreprise. « Toronto est l’une des plus grandes métropoles du monde : une ville innovante, diversifiée et résolument tournée vers l’avenir. Nous sommes fiers d’introduire le Waymo Driver dans la plus grande ville du Canada et de collaborer avec les communautés dynamiques des affaires, des arts et de la culture qui partagent notre engagement envers des rues plus sécuritaires et une mobilité plus accessible. »Pour assurer notre service à Toronto, nous faisons équipe avec Element Fleet Management, une entreprise dont le siège social se trouve à Toronto et qui est un leader mondial des solutions intelligentes de gestion de flottes et de mobilité. Element nous fournira des services complets de gestion de flottes. Avec Element et nos autres partenaires, nous investirons progressivement dans la création de centaines d’emplois liés à l’entretien de la flotte, aux essais sur route, au service à la clientèle et à d’autres activités nécessaires à l’exploitation de notre service. Ce partenariat s’inscrit dans la continuité des liens que Waymo a déjà tissés avec le Canada, notamment avec l’Office d’investissement du régime de pensions du Canada (Investissements RPC), un investisseur de longue date, et Magna International, son partenaire manufacturier.« En tant qu’entreprise canadienne, nous sommes fiers d’élargir notre partenariat avec Waymo afin de contribuer à l’arrivée des services de transport de personnes à la demande par véhicules autonomes à Toronto, a déclaré Laura Dottori-Attanasio, présidente et cheffe de la direction d’Element Fleet Management. Ensemble, Element et Waymo contribueront à créer des possibilités d’emploi en mettant à profit l’expertise d’Element en gestion de flottes, ses capacités opérationnelles et ses solutions de mobilité intelligente pour soutenir le déploiement à grande échelle de flottes de véhicules autonomes, tout en assurant la fiabilité de leurs opérations. »Toronto figure parmi les régions métropolitaines dont la croissance est la plus rapide en Amérique du Nord. Les besoins en matière de mobilité y évoluent et les options de transport se multiplient. Des pistes cyclables au transport en commun, le Waymo Driver, conçu pour fonctionner par tous les temps, pourrait offrir une option supplémentaire en complément des moyens de transport existants. Selon les données recueillies sur plus de 400 millions de kilomètres parcourus en conduite entièrement autonome, les véhicules Waymo ont été impliqués dans 95 % moins d’accidents entraînant des blessures graves ou plus graves que les véhicules conduits par des humains dans les villes où le service est offert. Cela représente 20 fois moins d’accidents de ce type.La sécurité et l’accessibilité sont à la base de la mission de Waymo : devenir le service de conduite autonome auquel le public fait le plus confiance au monde. Nous sommes fiers de collaborer avec des organismes de premier plan qui œuvrent en faveur de l’accessibilité et de la mobilité, notamment BALANCE for Blind Adults, l’Institut national canadien pour les aveugles (INCA), Community Living Toronto, Connected Canadians et Epilepsy Ontario.« L’innovation qui favorise l’autonomie est au cœur de tout ce que nous faisons. L’expérience de Waymo en matière de collaboration avec des personnes ayant une déficience visuelle pour concevoir des solutions accessibles est encourageante. Sa décision de nous consulter dès le début montre qu’une telle approche peut donner des résultats concrets », a déclaré Michelle McQuigge, PDG de BALANCE for Blind Adults.Nous sommes ravis d’aider les résidents et les visiteurs à découvrir tout ce que Toronto a à offrir. Si vous avez envie de faire l’essai du Waymo Driver à Toronto, inscrivez-vous pour recevoir nos mises à jour et être parmi les premiers informés du lancement de notre service : waymo.com/waymo-in-canada.

comments.textZhHtml: 我认为缺乏任何人参与是对很多人的吸引力的一部分。较低的成本也确实有所帮助，不过，我认为看看由于缺乏司机而带来的名义价格优势是否会随着时间的推移而得到证实，这将会很有趣。

只有当存在具有较高转换成本的俘虏/粘性受众时，才会出现Enshitification。 “载你从 A 到 B”没有护城河，他们将继续在品质和价格上竞争。 在维加斯，目前有 3 家（很快将有 4 家以上）无人驾驶出租车服务正在运营。

此外，你不能一边抱怨向大公司提供资金，一边赞扬一项需要大量研发资金才能推向市场的出色服务。 车库里没有两个人能够独自创办一家自动驾驶汽车公司或一家超音速喷气式飞机公司。 发射卫星、制造汽车、建设数据中心等都需要大量资金。

仅仅因为 Waymo 脏、臭、吵，你愿意花几千万在一个城市推出自己的自动驾驶车队（这个价格就只有一辆！而且没有研发！）？

comments.author: vlovich123
comments.textZhHtml: 不正确。当他们出于任何原因（价格竞争、利润提高等）而降低服务质量以提高利润时，也会发生Enshittification。这就是为什么最便宜的级别车辆的质量会更差，所有服务都会像这样运行，因为这就是你在这个价位上所能实现的一切（除非他们弄清楚如何拥有自动化的分布式清洁站，即使这样，这也很棘手，因为汽车仍然无法使用，并且即使只是绕了一小段路，你也会因为清洁而损失金钱）。

comments.author: refurb
comments.textZhHtml:
Enshitification只是对价格敏感的消费者愿意以质量换取价格。

如果它真的伤害了公司，他们就会停止这样做

comments.author: vlovich123
comments.textZhHtml:
不一定。它还意味着将市场细分到极致，这样即使质量的微小提高也会带来显着更高的价格。这是为了让对价格最敏感的客户获得最差的质量，而对价格不敏感的客户则可以通过大幅增加成本获得稍微更好的产品。

我仍然相信，虽然在这种模式中价值提取更高，但人们普遍希望生活的世界是企业以这种方式进行价格歧视的能力不会那么肆无忌惮的世界。

stories.title: How the Claude Code team does code review
stories.titleZh: Claude Code 团队如何进行代码审查
stories.author: pretext

comments.author: avinoth
comments.textZhHtml:
这就像 Google 的基础设施博客之一。谷歌规模的东西只与他们相关并且适合他们。我们从较小的工程团队那里吸取了很多惨痛的教训，他们遵循的过程是“谷歌就是这样做的”。

同样，Anthropic 也有能力做到这一点，因为他们拥有几乎无限的代币和实验室来训练针对其特定用例的模型。我们其他人需要代码理解，以免我们变得依赖于持续供应代币（这是这些实验室非常希望实现的状态）

因此，除非您在实验室工作，或者在公司的整个生命周期内保证拥有无限的代币，否则继续阅读代码而不是让每个工程师 30k PR 成为常态，对公司和您都有好处。

文章的摘录表明了我的观点

>团队成员的头脑中保留着 Claude Code 的完整心理模型，我们认为任何人都不需要这样做。当有人想要理解代码库的一部分时，他们会要求 Claude 为该部分编写一个解释器。它需要几分钟的时间并反映当前的代码。

comments.author: thatsabadlook
comments.textZhHtml:
即便如此，我们真的有证据表明他们所做的事情对他们来说是合理的或实用的吗？他们的正常运行时间接近 3 个 9，泄露的克劳德代码看起来像汤，大量的安全问题，他们无法构建沙箱来拯救他们的公司，最后我听说，如果不调整任意事情的数字，他们甚至无法盈利。

我认为我很擅长听取不赚钱的公司的建议。

comments.author: avinoth
comments.textZhHtml: 正是如此。他们不断地重复着这样的故事：软件工程就应该是这样的。始终依赖代币。不用担心正常运行时间或错误 - 代理可以解决它，不用担心安全性 - 代理可以解决它，不用担心代码理解 - 代理将永远为您服务。

comments.author: oblio
comments.textZhHtml:
> 代理商将永远为您服务。

2000 年左右，罗马尼亚的一家投资基金 (FNI) 投放了一些超级著名的广告，上面写着“FNI is Watch”（FNI 正在注视）。

6 个月后，他们破产了。

comments.author: samuell
comments.textZhHtml: 成功了

comments.author: panarky
comments.textZhHtml:
如果他们的现金流为正，75% 的计算用于研究和培训，那么您认为当他们转向 50-50 训练推理时，现金流会发生什么？

因为“调整前沿”更多的是打开印钞机开关，而不是安全。

comments.author: thr0w
comments.textZhHtml:
> 他们要求克劳德为那个切片写一个解释器

如果他们的克劳德和我们的克劳德一样，那么这是一个笑话。克劳德的写作风格令人心智麻木。需要不断地推动它才能用易于理解的英语解释事物。

comments.author: bulbar
comments.textZhHtml:
它还混合了重要和不重要的信息。它倾向于认为提交/错误修复很重要，并且很乐意将其与功能的重要属性一起列出。

至少 Opus 5.5 做到了这一点。不过，它的写作比其他模型要好。我让其他模型用难以理解的语言解释了一些东西，技术上是正确的，但实际上并不是什么内容。

comments.author: engine_y
comments.textZhHtml:
它就像试图用评论中的诗歌来打动你： 
“该函数的作用是，它做得很好，而且只执行一次”

comments.author: froggy
comments.textZhHtml: 尝试让它解释“ISO 普通语言标准”中的某些内容。昨天这对我来说发生了巨大的变化。语言将从密集的大段落变为措辞简单的2-3句段落。不过我使用的是 gpt。

comments.author: meheleventyone
comments.textZhHtml: 在我看来，即使让它写得不那么迟钝的英语也是不够的。以易于理解的方式构建文档似乎存在真正的问题。此外，它也是一个真正的恶魔，会将其上下文作为隐式假设泄露到文档中。

comments.author: panarky
comments.textZhHtml: v5.5 消除了早期版本中许多难以理解的散文。

> v5.5

当 5.5 用一堵文字墙回应并且你陷入第一个乏味的句子时，你是否仍然感到精神上的摩擦？前几天我什至让它生成了一个语法无效的英语句子。还是很糟糕。
